reason: The quote says Transit Gateway #2 incurs no data processing charges for data from a peering attachment and, as inbound inter-Region transfer is free, no further charges apply on the Oregon side.
The quote states the AWS Network Firewall owner is billed hourly for network function attachments.
The quote states data processing charges do not apply for data sent from a peering attachment to a Transit Gateway.
The quote speaks of a partial VPC Transit Gateway hour only; the claim generalizes to every transit gateway attachment hour (VPN, peering, Connect and others), which the quote does not state.
The quote states each Transit Gateway owner is billed hourly for the peering attachment with the other Transit Gateway.
The quote under the Pricing example heading states data processing is charged to the VPC owner who sends the traffic to Transit Gateway.
The quote states standard AWS data transfer charges are incurred in addition to any Transit Gateway charges.
The quote states the VPC account owner is billed hourly for each hour their VPCs are attached to a Transit Gateway.
The quote states the Transit Gateway owner is billed hourly for AWS VPN attachments.
The quote states each attachment can be associated with one route table and can propagate its routes to one or more route tables.
The quote states Connect attachment routes are propagated by default and that with a VPC you must create static routes to send traffic to the transit gateway.
The quote gives all three behaviors: VPN routes propagated via BGP, Direct Connect gateway allowed prefixes originated via BGP, and a static route needed for a peering attachment.
Row 'Attachments per transit gateway | 5,000 | Yes' under header Name | Default | Adjustable.
Row 'CIDR blocks per transit gateway | 5 | No' under header Name | Default | Adjustable.
Row gives 'Up to 5 Gbps' per Connect peer (GRE tunnel) per Connect attachment, Adjustable No.
Row gives 'Up to 300,000' maximum packets per second per Connect peer, Adjustable No.
Row 'Connect peers (GRE tunnels) per Connect attachment | 4 | No'.
Row 'Direct Connect gateways per transit gateway | 20 | No'.
Row gives up to 100 Gbps each direction per Direct Connect gateway or peered transit gateway connection per available AZ, with the contact-SA/TAM adjustable note.
Row gives up to 7,500,000 packets per second per Direct Connect and peering attachment per available AZ in the Region.
Row 'Transit gateways per account | 5 | Yes' under header Name | Default | Adjustable.
Row 'Transit gateways per Direct Connect gateway | 6 | No'.
Row 'Transit gateways per VPC | 5 | No'.
Row 'Peering attachments per transit gateway | 50 | Yes'.
Row gives 1 peering attachment between two transit gateways or between a transit gateway and a Cloud WAN CNE, Adjustable No.
Row 'Pending peering attachments per transit gateway | 10 | Yes'.
Row 'Transit gateway route tables per transit gateway | 20 | Yes'.
The row gives 1 static route for a prefix to a single attachment, but the claim's framing 'a transit gateway route table can hold' adds a per-route-table scope that the row does not state.
Row gives a default of 10,000 total combined routes across all route tables of a single transit gateway.
Row gives up to 100 Gbps each direction per VPC attachment per Availability Zone.
Row gives up to 7,500,000 packets per second per transit gateway VPC attachment per Availability Zone.
The quote on the Transit Gateway quotas page states each quota is Region-specific unless otherwise noted.
The quote states Transit Gateway is a Regional resource that can connect thousands of VPCs within the same Region.

The quote line under 'Route evaluation order' names the most specific route, but that it is evaluated first comes only from its list position and the intro sentence in the surrounding text, not from the quote.
The quote lists VPC, VPN, VPN Concentrator, Client VPN, Direct Connect gateway, Peering and Connect attachments as supported and says an attachment can be propagated to multiple route tables.
The quote recommends a separate subnet per VPC attachment with a small CIDR such as /28 so more addresses remain for EC2 resources.
The quote states security group referencing only works if enabled for both the transit gateway and its VPC attachments.
The quote states cross-referencing works in inbound rules only, outbound rules do not support it, and there are no additional costs.
The quote states referencing is not supported across transit gateway peering and both VPCs must be attached to the same transit gateway.
The quote states referencing is not supported for PrivateLink endpoints and recommends IP CIDR-based rules instead.
The quote states that with an inspection VPC, referencing through the transit gateway does not work across Gateway Load Balancer or Network Firewall.
The quote states referencing is not supported for VPC attachments in the Availability Zone use1-az3.
On the page about accepting a Transit Gateway resource share, the quote says an added account receives an invitation and must accept in the AWS RAM console before accessing the shared resources.
The quote states AWS RAM can share a transit gateway for VPC attachments across accounts or across an organization in AWS Organizations.

The quote supports showing only the preferred route and the backup appearing when the active route is withdrawn, but which path is the backup (Site-to-Site VPN behind Direct Connect) stands only in the following sentences, not in the quote.
The quote states the static route has higher priority for the same destination, so the propagated route is not included.
The quote recommends a unique ASN for each transit gateway in multi-gateway deployments and mentions inter-Region peering.
The quote states one subnet per enabled AZ, a network interface placed in it, and traffic routable to all subnets in that AZ, not just the specified one.
The quote states one subnet per AZ is specified, these are entry and exit points, and other subnets are reached only if the attachment subnets have routes to them.

The first quote supports the failed case, but the second quote ('The VPC attachment remains visible for 2 hours') does not say deleted; the deleted state stands only in the bullet label in the surrounding text.
The two quotes state VPC CIDR blocks are propagated to the transit gateway route table and that you can't filter on advertised routes.
The quote states you must add a route to the subnet route table for traffic to route through the transit gateway.
The quote states a Site-to-Site VPN attachment connects VPCs and on-premises networks and supports dynamic and static routes and IPv4 and IPv6.
Under the Shared transit gateways > Considerations heading, the quote states a Site-to-Site VPN attachment must be created in the account that owns the transit gateway.
The quote only says each spoke VPC connects to the Transit Gateway to reach other VPCs; the comparison with VPC peering and avoiding a mesh as VPC count grows are not in the quote.
Under the REL02-BP04 heading 'Prefer hub-and-spoke topologies over many-to-many mesh', the quote says the hub centralizes connections and enhances operability, scalability and control.
The quote says to place the hub in the organization's Network Services account so network engineers manage it centrally.
The quote describes Transit Gateway as managed, scalable and highly available for hub-and-spoke networks with segmentation, centralized routing and simplified connection.
The quote says to provide routes only between networks that should communicate and omit others, for example separate workloads with no inter-dependencies.
The claim restates the quote 'Transit Gateway enables customers to connect thousands of VPCs.'
The quote names traffic inspection, interface VPC endpoint access and NAT gateway or instance egress as shared services centralized through the hub.
The quote supports the first clause, but 'centralizes network and security posture constructs in a single place' stands only in later sentences of the paragraph, not in the quote.
The quote supports only that segments are routing domains allowing communication within a segment by default; centralizing constructs and segmenting by policy are in another paragraph, not the quote.
The quote states Transit Gateway consolidates the VPC routing configuration for a Region in a hub-and-spoke design and each spoke connects only to it.
The quote states thousands of VPCs and all hybrid connectivity (VPN and Direct Connect) attach to one gateway, consolidating routing configuration in one place.
The quote states route tables, associations and propagations segment traffic, managing routing domains such as production and non-production that cannot communicate.
The quote states the hub-and-spoke model simplifies management and reduces operational costs because VPCs only connect to the Transit Gateway.
The Architecture row under the six-column header gives each value named in the claim.
The row for Direct Connect + Transit Gateway gives the use case 'Dedicated network connection over private lines to regional router for multiple VPCs'.
The Latency row gives Lowest for VPC peering, extra due to VPN encryption for transit VPC, and an additional hop for Transit Gateway.
The Scope row gives Regional/Global, Regional, Regional, Regional, Global, Regional in the claimed column order.
The Segmentation row gives security groups, TGW route tables, no segmentation, segments and service network policies for the named columns.
The row for Transit Gateway + Site-to-Site VPN gives the use case 'AWS managed IPsec VPN connection over the internet to regional router for multiple VPCs'.
The quote states Transit Gateway traffic always stays on the AWS backbone, never traverses the public internet, reducing exploits and DDoS threats.
The quote lists higher appliance costs on EC2, limited throughput per VPN connection and overhead because customers manage HA and redundancy.
The quote states a hub VPC connects to every spoke VPC through VPN and contains EC2 instances running appliances that route over the VPN overlay.
The quote introduces the list of services that integrate with PrivateLink and says a VPC endpoint connects to them privately as if in your VPC.
Both quotes state 10 Gbps per AZ by default per endpoint with automatic scaling up to 100 Gbps.
The quote states the maximum across all AZs is the AZ count multiplied by 100 Gbps and to contact AWS support for more.
The two quotes state S3 supports IPv6 for gateway and interface VPC endpoints and that it is available at no additional cost.
